The **Green Eyes plot** (or Green Eye Iris plot, Crocetta, Irpino, Antonucci
and Marin, 2025) is a compact picture of *all the distributions observed on a
single statistical unit*. It was introduced to display the satisfaction of
the customers of a service with respect to several aspects, but it can be used
for any row of a distributional data table.

```{r}
library(DistrViz)
library(DDAWASS)
library(ggplot2)

data(univer, package = "CUB")
univer$Faculty <- factor(sprintf("F%02d", univer$faculty))
univer$Gender  <- factor(univer$gender, levels = 0:1, labels = c("M", "W"))
items <- c("informat", "willingn", "officeho", "compete", "global")
M <- data2MatD(univer, unit = c("Faculty", "Gender"), vars = items,
               support = 1:7, min.n = 10)
dv <- dv_data(M, ranges = c(1, 7))
```

## Reading a Green Eyes plot

Each variable is a **sector** of a circle. Inside the sector the cumulative
distribution function of the variable is drawn radially, from the inner
circle (the grey *pupil*, cdf = 0) to the outer circle (cdf = 1): the
radial thickness of each coloured band is the probability of a value, and its
colour is the position of the value in the range of the variable (dark red for
the lowest ratings, dark green for the highest ones).

```{r, fig.width = 4.5, fig.height = 4.5, out.width = "60%", fig.align = "center"}
gei_plot(dv, row = "F02_W")
```

The dashed circle is at cdf = 0.5: the colour crossing it is the colour of
the **median**. A group whose eye is dark green near the pupil has many
high ratings and few low ones: it has "green eyes". Red and orange bands near
the pupil reveal a share of dissatisfied respondents.

Compare the eye above with the one of a group with lower satisfaction:

```{r, fig.width = 4.5, fig.height = 4.5, out.width = "60%", fig.align = "center"}
gei_plot(dv, row = "F13_M")
```

## Variability and skewness

`show_sd = TRUE` adds, in each sector, a radial bar centred on the median
circle whose length is proportional to the standard deviation of the
distribution (relative to the largest standard deviation observed for that
variable among all the units). `show_skewness = TRUE` adds a tangential tick
at radial position $(\sqrt[3]{\gamma} + 3)/6$, where $\gamma$ is the skewness:
ticks inside the median circle mark left-skewed distributions (a long tail
of low ratings), ticks outside mark right-skewed ones.

```{r, fig.width = 4.5, fig.height = 4.5, out.width = "60%", fig.align = "center"}
gei_plot(dv, row = "F13_M", show_sd = TRUE, show_skewness = TRUE)
```

## Order of the sectors

By default the sectors follow the order of the columns. Since neighbouring
sectors are compared at a glance, it helps to put **similar variables next to
each other**. Two automatic orders are available.

With `var_order = "tsp"` (alias `"hamiltonian"`) the variables are the nodes of
a complete graph whose edges are weighted by the correlation distance
$$d(X_j, X_k) = \sqrt{2\,[1 - r(X_j, X_k)]},$$
where $r$ is the Wasserstein correlation, and the order is the **shortest
Hamiltonian cycle** through the variables (a Travelling Salesman Problem).
Since the sectors lie on a circle, the last variable is adjacent to the
first one, and a cycle is exactly what is needed. `dv_var_order()` returns the
cycle and its length:

```{r}
tsp <- dv_var_order(dv)
tsp$labels
round(tsp$dist, 2)
```

The cycle is computed exactly for up to 9 variables, and with a heuristic
(nearest-neighbour and random tours improved by 2-opt) for more variables.

```{r, fig.width = 4.5, fig.height = 4.5, out.width = "60%", fig.align = "center"}
gei_plot(dv, row = "F13_M", var_order = "tsp")
```

With `var_order = "cluster"` the order is the one of a hierarchical clustering
of the variables (see `dv_cluster()`); a permutation of the variables can be
given as well.

## Many units: `gei_grid()`

`gei_grid()` draws one eye per unit. Units can be shown in the order of the
data, ordered by a hierarchical clustering (`order = "cluster"`), or sorted
by a partition given in `groups`, whose labels are reported in the facet
labels. Here we use the Ward clustering of **DDAWASS**:

```{r, fig.height = 6.2}
hc <- WD_hclust(M, method = "ward.D2")
gei_grid(dv, groups = cutree(hc, 3), ncol = 7)
```

The three clusters are immediately recognizable: cluster 2 collects the
groups with "green eyes", cluster 3 the faculties (F06, F13) with a large share
of low ratings, cluster 1 the intermediate situations.

The same can be done with the k-means of **DDAWASS**:

```{r, fig.height = 6.2}
km <- WD_kmeans(M, k = 3, rep = 20)
gei_grid(dv, groups = km$solution$IDX, ncol = 7)
```

A subset of units can be selected with `rows`, by index or by name:

```{r, fig.height = 2.8}
gei_grid(dv, rows = c("F02_M", "F02_W", "F13_M", "F13_W"), ncol = 4)
```

## Difference eyes: where a unit departs from the others

A Green Eyes plot shows the distributions of a unit; it does not tell, at a
glance, *how* they differ from those of the other units. `gei_diff()` draws a
**difference eye**: sectors and radius are those of a Green Eyes plot (the
radius is the probability level $t$, from $t = 0$ at the pupil to $t = 1$ at
the border), but the colour is the difference between the quantile function
of the unit and that of a reference,
$$D_{ij}(t) = Q_{ij}(t) - \bar{Q}_j(t),$$
red where the unit is below the reference, green where it is above, white
where they coincide. By default the reference is the Wasserstein barycenter
of all the units, whose quantile function is the mean of the quantile
functions.

```{r, fig.height = 6.5}
gei_diff(dv, order = "cluster", var_order = "tsp", ncol = 7)
```

The picture separates the groups that are below the mean profile at every
probability level (F13, F06: red from the pupil to the border) from those that
are above it (F02, F05), and those whose difference is concentrated in one
part of the distribution. For instance, the eyes of F07 are green except in
one sector, where a red band near the pupil reveals a tail of low ratings that
the other aspects do not have. The outer border is almost white everywhere:
all the groups have some top ratings, and the differences are in the low and
central part of the distributions.

Difference eyes are a picture of the **Wasserstein variance**. The variance of
variable $j$ is the mean over the units of
$\int_0^1 D_{ij}(t)^2\,dt$, so the "amount of colour" in a sector is the
contribution of that cell to the variance. The differences used for the plot
are returned in the attribute `"diff"`:

```{r}
D <- attr(gei_diff(dv, levels = 1000), "diff")
contr <- apply(D^2, c(1, 2), mean)            # units x variables
rbind(from_eyes = colMeans(contr), WD.var.covar = diag(WD.var.covar(M)))
round(sort(rowSums(contr) / sum(contr), decreasing = TRUE)[1:5], 3)
```

The five groups above account for almost half of the total variance.

The reference can also be a unit or a group of units (their barycenter). Here
the groups of faculties F13 and F06 are compared with the barycenter of the
"green eyes" cluster found above:

```{r, fig.height = 3.6}
green <- names(which(cutree(hc, 3) == cutree(hc, 3)["F02_W"]))
gei_diff(dv, rows = c("F13_M", "F13_W", "F06_M", "F06_W"), reference = green,
         var_order = "tsp", ncol = 4, labels = TRUE)
```

With variables on different scales, `scale = "sd"` (the default in that case)
divides the differences by the Wasserstein standard deviation of each
variable; `scale = "range"` by its range.

## Eyes on a factorial plane

`gei_pca()` draws the eye of each unit at its position on a factorial plane.
By default it computes the quantile-based multiple factor analysis of all the
variables (`DDAWASS::WD.MultiplePCA()` for discrete distributions,
`HistDAWass::WH.MultiplePCA()` for histograms), but any result with the
coordinates of the units in `$ind$coord` (or a matrix of coordinates) can be
given. The diameter of the eyes is `size` (default 0.1) times the smallest of
the width and the height of the cloud of points, so that an eye never takes
more than one tenth of the plane in either direction. The outline of the eyes
can be coloured by a partition.

```{r, fig.height = 5}
mfa <- WD.MultiplePCA(M, items, quantiles = 10, plots = FALSE)
gei_pca(dv, mfa, var_order = "tsp", groups = cutree(hc, 3))
```

On the right, a **key** shows the eye of the barycenter of all the units with
the names of the variables around the sectors; with `key = "groups"` (and
`groups`) there is one key eye for the barycenter (prototype) of each group,
and `key = "none"` removes it. For discrete distributions the barycenter is
projected on the observed support (`DDAWASS::WD.vec.mean.simplified()`).

```{r, fig.height = 5}
gei_pca(dv, mfa, var_order = "tsp", groups = cutree(hc, 3), key = "groups")
```

The first axis orders the groups from the least satisfied (on the left, where
red and orange appear around the pupil) to the most satisfied ones (on the
right). Other axes can be chosen with `axes`, and the eyes can be made larger
with `size`:

```{r, fig.height = 5}
gei_pca(dv, mfa, axes = c(1, 3), size = 0.15, var_order = "tsp", labels = FALSE)
```

### Interactive version

With many units the eyes overlap. With `interactive = TRUE` (and the
**ggiraph** package installed) `gei_pca()` returns an interactive plot:

* hovering an eye shows a tooltip with the name of the unit, its group and its
  coordinates (over a band of the eye, also the variable, the value and its
  probability), and fades the other eyes;
* clicking an eye hides it and leaves its point of application, drawn in red;
  clicking the point shows the eye again. The lasso buttons of the toolbar
  hide (or show again) all the eyes in an area, and the reset button shows all
  of them;
* the zoom button activates zooming (mouse wheel) and panning (drag);
* above the plot, two switches show or hide the dashed median circles and the
  names of all the units, and a slider changes the size of all the eyes (each
  eye is rescaled around its point of application); the eye under the mouse
  comes on top of the others;
* `hidden` gives the units whose eyes are hidden at start.

Try it below (the eyes of F02_M and F02_W, the most satisfied groups, are
hidden at start: only their red points are visible on the right):

```{r, eval = has_cub && requireNamespace("ggiraph", quietly = TRUE), fig.height = 5}
gei_pca(dv, mfa, var_order = "tsp", groups = cutree(hc, 3), key = "groups",
        interactive = TRUE, hidden = c("F02_M", "F02_W"), width_svg = 8)
```

The controls above the plot can be removed with `controls = FALSE`, and the
range of the size slider is set by `size_range`. In a Shiny app the hidden
units are returned in `input$<outputId>_selected`.

## Customizing the plot

The result is a `ggplot` object, which can be modified with the usual
**ggplot2** tools. The main options are the palette, the size and colour of
the pupil, the median circle, and the background:

```{r, fig.height = 3}
gei_grid(dv, rows = c("F02_W", "F13_M", "F06_W"), ncol = 3,
         palette = "Hiroshige", reverse = TRUE, pupil = 0.5, pupil_color = "white",
         median_line = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Hiroshige palette, white pupil")
```

With `polar = FALSE` the eye is "unrolled" into stacked bars, which makes it
easier to read the probabilities:

```{r, fig.width = 5, fig.height = 4, out.width = "70%", fig.align = "center"}
gei_plot(dv, row = "F13_M", polar = FALSE)
```

## Histogram data

Green Eyes plots also work with matrices of histograms: each histogram is
discretized into `n_levels` classes (see the first vignette).

```{r, fig.height = 3.5}
gei_grid(HistDAWass::BLOOD, rows = 1:6, ncol = 6, n_levels = 15,
         palette = "Zissou 1")
```

## Reference

Crocetta C., Irpino A., Antonucci L., Marin C. (2025). A performance indicator
and its decomposition according to the impacts of different aspects based on
distributional data. *Quality & Quantity*, 59(3), 2091-2110.
doi:10.1007/s11135-024-01956-0
